statements.body: The project is named Teatime Post.
The operator publishes a fortnightly tea-tasting newsletter.
The current subscriber base is approximately 300 people.
The operator drafts newsletter content in plain text.
The operator wants to store and manage a subscriber list.
The operator wants subscribers to be able to join or leave via a link, without operator involvement.
The operator wants to send an issue to all subscribers by triggering a single action.
The tool will do exactly three things: manage the subscriber list, handle self-serve subscribe and unsubscribe via link, and send the drafted issue on demand — nothing else in this phase.

concerns.coverage: The operator currently lacks a dedicated tool combining subscriber list management, self-serve opt-in/opt-out, and one-action sending; the gap is implied by the request to build one.
A single operator authors and sends the newsletter; roughly 300 subscribers receive it. No other roles or collaborators are mentioned.
Operator drafts in plain text, then triggers a send action; subscribers join or leave autonomously via a link. Entry point is the operator hitting go; exit point is delivery to the subscriber list.
The operator explicitly stated this is genuinely all they want; anything beyond subscriber management, subscribe/unsubscribe links, and issue sending is out of scope for this phase.
The system must hold a subscriber list (at minimum email addresses). Volume is ~300 records. No retention, export, or sensitivity expectations have been stated yet.
Unsubscribe must be self-serve and reliable to avoid trapping unwilling recipients. No other safety or abuse concerns have been stated yet.

candidates.body: What observable outcome would tell you this tool worked — for example, every fortnightly issue sent with one action and zero manual list edits?
candidates.whySelected: Success is the only uncovered core concern; without observable evidence of success the framing cannot close, and the answer directly bounds what the first slice must demonstrate.

candidates.body: How will the tool actually deliver email — through your own SMTP setup, an existing email-sending service, or something you have not decided yet?
candidates.whySelected: Delivery mechanism is the largest unstated constraint and dominates the shape of the first vertical slice, though it does not fill the uncovered success concern.

candidates.body: If a send fails partway through the 300 recipients, is it acceptable to just retry manually, or do you need the tool to track and resume delivery?
candidates.whySelected: Partial-send failure is the most likely operational pain for a one-action bulk send; the answer bounds how much delivery bookkeeping the first slice needs.

readyAdvice.why: The success concern is still uncovered — there is no stated observable evidence that the tool worked — and the delivery mechanism, a slice-defining constraint, is unstated. One or two more answers should make the seed sufficient.

statements.body: A successful send takes under five minutes of operator time from triggering to completion.
Zero subscriber address leaks per send is a required success condition.
Unsubscribes must complete without any operator involvement, ever.

concerns.coverage: The operator can observe success when: each issue sends within five minutes of operator time, no subscriber addresses are leaked, and unsubscribes resolve without operator involvement.
Zero address leaks per send is now an explicit operator requirement, not just a best-practice concern; accidental exposure of the subscriber list is a named failure mode.

candidates.body: Do you have any hard constraints on how the emails actually get sent — such as budget limits, willingness to pay for a third-party sending service, or a requirement to self-host?
candidates.whySelected: Every approved statement describes what the tool does, but nothing bounds the environment it must live in. The sending mechanism is the largest unresolved cost and design driver: a third-party email API versus self-hosted SMTP leads to very different builds, and deliverability at 300 recipients is nontrivial from a raw server. This single answer bounds the first vertical slice more than any other open question.

candidates.body: Who fixes things when a send fails or a subscribe link breaks — is it you alone, and how quickly does it need to be back up before the next fortnightly issue?
candidates.whySelected: Operations is thinly covered: the ledger names a single operator but says nothing about maintenance, failure handling, or tolerance for downtime. Since issues are fortnightly, the answer may reveal that very cheap operational choices are acceptable, which strongly shapes the slice.

candidates.body: How tolerable is imperfect delivery at the start — for example, is it acceptable if a handful of the 300 subscribers land in spam or miss an issue during the first few sends?
candidates.whySelected: Quality has no approved coverage. Deliverability tolerance determines whether the first slice can use a simple sending path or must invest in domain authentication and bounce handling immediately.

readyAdvice.why: The scope, success criteria, and safety requirements are well ratified, but the seed has no constraints on hosting, budget, or sending infrastructure and no operations or quality coverage. Answering the sending-constraints question would likely make the first slice buildable; until then, the design space is unbounded in its most expensive dimension.
